# MapMaker lessons on the Support Hub (questions, layers and sources)
Built 2026-11-11 from the lesson files by the MapMaker resource pages, Vera knowledge builder 1.6. Do not edit by hand; edit the lesson files and rebuild.

How to use this file: each lesson below has its own MapMaker map. When a teacher names one of these lessons (by title or lesson ID) and asks for new or different questions, base every question only on the bookmarks, layers and pop-up content listed for that lesson, and use bookmark and layer names exactly as written. If a request needs information that lesson's map does not show, say so plainly instead of inventing it. Use only the links listed for that lesson. The answers to the lessons' questions are not in this file: do not give them, and do not write student material that contains them.

### 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles
**Lesson ID:** revolutionary-battles-1775-1776
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Road to revolution and the Revolution. **Time:** About 62 minutes: 52 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=bda07736a1b9425ea19fdde282088bd6)
**Description:** Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Social Studies.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Locate the 21 battles of 1775–1776 on the map and sort them by year, using the pop-up dates and the legend for the winner.
- Measure straight-line distances between Boston, Concord, New York, Philadelphia and Trenton with the Measure tool.
- Identify the major ports between Boston and Charleston from the Key Port Cities layer and the coastline, and explain what a navy based at New York could reach.
- Trace the end of 1776 through the numbered Turning Points and the Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton pop-ups.
- Use evidence from at least two places on the map to explain why the fighting moved from Boston to New York and across New Jersey.
**Bookmarks in this map:** Massachusetts.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Revolutionary War Battles: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates, a picture and a short account. The winner is shown only by the diamond's color, as listed in the legend (American Victory or British Victory); the pop-up does not state it in words; source: American Battlefield Trust.
- Revolutionary War Battlefields: Battlefield boundaries (gray) and the core areas where the fighting was heaviest (diagonal stripes). No pop-ups; source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program.
- Turning Points: Five white circles numbered 1 to 5, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, that appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the event's name, year, a short account (the Battle_details field) and the victor; source: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources.
- Thirteen British Colonies: Colony areas and borders in 1763, with each colony's name printed on the map. Colonies have no pop-up; source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988).
- 1763 Proclamation Line: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlement and land purchases, reserving the land beyond it for American Indian nations; source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988); the reservation is in the Proclamation's text ([Avalon Project, Yale Law School](https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/proc1763.asp)).
- Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off when the map opens): Ports that supplied armies and moved troops, from New England to the Caribbean and Britain. The legend separates a Major Port City (larger symbol) from a smaller Port. Each pop-up gives the port's name; the layer has no labels; source: Jay Feyerabend, [master's thesis](https://commons.lib.jmu.edu/masters202029/74), James Madison University (2021).
**What students read before they start:** British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Diamonds mark battles. A diamond's pop-up gives the battle's name, dates and story, but not the winner in words: the diamond's color shows the winner, so use the legend. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. White numbered circles are five turning points, numbered in the order they happened. A circle's pop-up is a short summary: it gives only the year and ends with a Victor line. Some circles sit on top of a diamond. Click there and use the arrows in the pop-up until the title is the battle you want. In the Key Port Cities layer, click a port to see its name; the legend tells a major port from a smaller one.
**Compelling question:** Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Where did the war begin? On the map: Open the Massachusetts bookmark. Click the blue diamond just left of circle 1. It is Lexington and Concord. Read its dates. Open the legend and check which color shows who won. Click circle 2. It covers the Boston diamond. Use the arrow in the pop-up until the title says Boston, then read its dates. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from circle 2 (Boston) to the blue diamond beside circle 1 (Concord). Answer: When was Lexington and Concord fought, and who won? How long did the siege of Boston last? How close to Boston did the war begin? Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: ________ miles
2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776? On the map: Zoom out one step from the Massachusetts bookmark. Drag the map from Quebec in the north to South Carolina in the south to find all 21 diamonds. If the diamonds disappear, you have zoomed out too far: zoom in one step. Click at least one diamond in each group and read its date line to see its year. Where diamonds overlap, zoom in. Read the colony's name printed on the map near each group of diamonds (colonies have no pop-up, and Quebec is not labeled). The diamonds around Boston are in Massachusetts: its name is printed farther north. Use the legend to see who won. Answer: Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?
3. Why New York? On the map: In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781. Use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port. Find the major ports between Boston and Charleston. Click each major port to read its name in the pop-up. Use Measure from New York to Philadelphia and from New York to Boston. Answer: Boston and Charleston are major ports: which other major ports lie between them? Using the distances you measured, what could a navy based at New York reach? New York to Philadelphia: ________ miles. New York to Boston: ________ miles
4. How did 1776 end? On the map: Open the New York/New Jersey bookmark. Click circles 4 and 5 and read each summary. Find the battles of Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. Circle 4 covers the Fort Washington and Fort Lee diamonds, and circle 5 covers Trenton. Click the circle and use the arrow in the pop-up until the title is the battle you want. Read each one's dates, and use the legend to see who won. To see the color of a covered diamond, zoom out until the circles disappear. Use Measure for the distance from circle 3 (Brooklyn, in New York City) to circle 5 (Trenton). Answer: When was each battle fought, and who won? How far from New York City had the fighting moved by the end of 1776? Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: ________ miles
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Trenton is one small American win after a run of British ones. Why do you think the map gives it its own turning point?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** siege, militia, Continental Army, Loyalist, harbor, campaign, retreat.
**Standards:** TX 8.4(C); TX 8.10(A); TX 8.10(C); FL SS.8.A.3.6; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.11.0, updated 2026-11-11.

### Roads, Trails, and Rails West
**Lesson ID:** roads-trails-and-rails-west
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny. **Time:** About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open Roads, Trails, and Rails West in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=3ec83a9d66454ade8aead0a64872d931)
**Description:** Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Indigenous Studies, Economics.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Identify where three of the seven trails started and ended from their pop-ups, and explain from the map why most began in Missouri.
- Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the Oregon Trail's length in its pop-up.
- Name Indigenous nations whose lands a trail crossed, using the Indigenous Territories layer.
- Compare the transcontinental railroad lines in the legend with the dotted trails to see which routes the railroads followed.
- Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how trails and then railroads changed the West, and for whom.
**Bookmarks in this map:** none.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Trails West: Seven trails west: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish, Santa Fe, Butterfield Overland and Pony Express, each a dotted line in its own color in the legend. Each pop-up is titled with the trail's name and gives a short history with places, dates and distances; source: National Geographic Education, from National Park Service trail information.
- Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911 (off when the map opens): Five transcontinental lines as thick colored lines named in the legend: Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific), Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) and Southern Pacific. No pop-up. In the Railroads group; source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team.
- Railroads 1826 to 1911 (off when the map opens): All railroad lines built from 1826 to 1911, as thin dark lines. Each pop-up gives the railroad's name (where recorded) and the year it was in operation by. In the Railroads group; source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team.
- Indigenous Territories (off when the map opens): Approximate territories of Indigenous nations, from a community-made map, each shaded in its own color with the nation's name appearing when zoomed in. Not listed in the legend. Click a territory to read the nation's name in the pop-up; source: Native Land Digital.
**What students read before they start:** In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people from the eastern United States went west in wagons, looking for farmland, gold or a place to practice their religion freely. A journey along one of the trails could take months. Later in the century, railroads were built across the West.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Each trail is a dotted line in its own color; the legend names them, and clicking a trail opens its pop-up. City and state names are part of the basemap. Railroads and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens: turn them on in Map layers. Thick colored lines are the transcontinental railroads, named in the legend, and thin dark lines are other railroads; of the railroads, only the thin lines have pop-ups. Zoomed out, the thin lines cover the East: zoom in to see single lines. Each Indigenous nation's territory is shaded in its own color; its name appears when you zoom in, or when you click the shading. The territories are approximate and aren't listed in the legend.
**Compelling question:** How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Where did the trails begin? On the map: Open the legend to see which color is which trail. Click three of the dotted trail lines. Read in each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Answer: Where did each trail start? In which state do most of them start, and why there? Use the Missouri River: zoom in between Kansas City and St. Louis to see its name.
2. How far, and how many? On the map: Find the Oregon Trail's color in the legend. Click the Oregon Trail in the state of Oregon, or near Boise in Idaho, where it runs alone. Check that the pop-up's title says Oregon Trail, then read its length and how many people traveled it. Find Kansas City, Missouri, on the basemap. Independence, where the trail began, is just east of it. Use Measure for a straight line from Kansas City to Portland, Oregon. Answer: How long was the Oregon Trail, and how many people traveled it? Why is the trail longer than a straight line? Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: ________ miles
3. Whose land? On the map: In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories. Zoom in until the nations' names appear. Follow one trail from one end to the other. Find two nations whose land it crossed: read the names on the map or click the shading. Answer: Which two nations' land did the trail cross? Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?
4. From trails to rails On the map: In Map layers, turn on Railroads. Zoom in on Nebraska, Wyoming and Utah until you can see single lines. The two thick lines that run from Omaha to Sacramento are the Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific): check them in the legend. Click a thin dark railroad line near one of the trails and read the year after Railroad in operation by: the railroad was running by that year. Answer: Which trails do the Transcontinental Railroad lines follow most closely? Was your thin line in operation before or after 1869, when the California Trail stopped being used? What does that suggest?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Pick one nation whose land a trail crossed. What would you want to ask someone who lived there in 1850?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** Manifest Destiny, emigrant, trail, transcontinental railroad, telegraph, Indigenous nation.
**Standards:** TX 8.6(B); TX 8.11(A); FL SS.8.A.4.1; C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.9.1, updated 2026-11-11.

### US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850
**Lesson ID:** us-slavery-and-slave-trade-1850
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Reform and the road to war. **Time:** About 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=cbee648b1f43455daae038b4bc64d6f4)
**Description:** Start with where slavery was legal in late 1850 and the line Congress drew in 1820. Then turn on, one layer at a time, the routes along which enslaved people were sold south, two ships whose captives took control, and the routes people followed to escape.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Civics, Social Studies.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the legend and pop-ups to place states and territories of late 1850 in four groups, and read the reason given for each.
- Explain what the Missouri Compromise line decided, and how Missouri and Utah Territory differ from its rule.
- Test an idea about the direction of the slave trade within the United States against the routes and their pop-ups.
- Follow the routes of La Amistad, the Creole and the Underground Railroad, and use a measured distance as evidence about safety in free states.
- Say what a map drawn from a 1920 atlas can and can't show about the people on these routes.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The United States in 1850; The South; The Ohio River and the North.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Underground Railroad cities (off when the map opens): Black dots for 69 cities on the Underground Railroad routes, three of them in Canada. The pop-up gives the city, its state or province and its country. Off when the map opens; source: Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), digitized by Esri.
- Underground Railroad approximate routes (off when the map opens): Green lines for the approximate routes that people escaping slavery followed. The lines have no names or dates. Off when the map opens; source: Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), digitized by Esri.
- Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841) (off when the map opens): Two dashed lines at sea (purple): the route of La Amistad in 1839 and of the Creole in 1841. The pop-up gives the direction and a short account. Off when the map opens; source: Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), digitized by Esri; accounts written for this map and fact-checked.
- Routes of the slave trade within the United States (off when the map opens): Black lines for the overland routes and the sea routes along which enslaved people were moved and sold. The pop-up gives the direction and a short account. Off when the map opens; source: Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), digitized by Esri; accounts written for this map and fact-checked.
- Missouri Compromise line: A dashed gray line at 36°30′ north, from southeastern Missouri west to the edge of New Mexico Territory. The pop-up gives the year and what the line meant; source: Esri, digitized from a public-domain map.
- Free and slave states and territories, 1850: The 31 states, the District of Columbia and seven territory areas of late 1850 in four groups: free state (dark blue), free territory (light blue), slave state and Washington, D.C. (dark orange), territory open to slavery (light orange). The pop-up gives the group, the year a newer state was admitted and a one-sentence reason; source: Harper's Atlas of American History (1920), digitized by Esri; groups and reasons from acts of Congress and state admission records, fact-checked 11 November 2026.
**What students read before they start:** In 1850 slavery was legal in some states and banned in others. A territory was land that belonged to the United States but was not yet a state. Twice, in 1820 and in 1850, Congress passed a compromise, an agreement where each side gives something up, about where slavery would be allowed. People who were enslaved were bought and sold, and many were forced to move far from their families. Some escaped. This map is traced from an atlas printed in 1920.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Dark blue: free state. Light blue: free territory. Dark orange: slave state, and Washington, D.C. Light orange: territory open to slavery. The dashed gray line is the Missouri Compromise line. Only these two layers are on at the start; turn on the others in Map layers when a question asks. Solid black lines are slave trade routes. The two dashed lines at sea are two ships. The thinner green lines and the black dots are the Underground Railroad. The legend names each one. No line has arrows: click it and the pop-up gives the direction. Small states may have no name on the map; click one to see it.
**Compelling question:** By 1850, how did slavery divide the United States, and what did that division mean for the people who were enslaved?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Four groups On the map: Open The United States in 1850 bookmark and open the legend. Click California, Texas, Oregon Territory and New Mexico Territory. Read the group at the top of each pop-up. Click New Jersey and read the sentence under its group. Answer: (a) Which group is each of these in: California, Texas, Oregon Territory, New Mexico Territory? (b) In which part of the country are the slave states? (c) New Jersey is shaded as a free state. What does its pop-up say about people still held there in 1850?
2. A line drawn in 1820 On the map: Click the dashed line. Read the year and the description. Click Missouri, the orange state just north of the east end of the dashed line (its name may not show). Read the sentence in its pop-up about the line. Click Unorganized territory and then Utah Territory. Read the reason in each pop-up. Look at where the dashed line ends in the west. Answer: (a) What did the line of 1820 decide? (b) How is Missouri an exception to it? (c) Unorganized territory and Utah Territory are both north of the line's latitude. Which law decided about slavery in each one, and what did it say?
3. Before the routes appear On the map: Open The South bookmark. Leave the other layers off. Write your idea down before you turn anything on. Answer: Inside the slave states, enslaved people were sold from one region to another. Which way do you think most of them were moved, and what makes you think so? I think most were moved from ______________ toward ______________ because ______________.
4. Sold south On the map: In Map layers, turn on Routes of the slave trade within the United States. Open The South bookmark. Click a black line on land. Read Direction people were moved and the account under it. Click a black line at sea and read its pop-up too. Answer: (a) In which direction were enslaved people moved, by land and by sea? (b) Name two states the pop-up gives as places people were taken from, and the kind of country they were taken to. (c) Near which city or state do many of the lines meet? (d) Was your idea in question 3 right?
5. Two ships On the map: In Map layers, turn off Routes of the slave trade within the United States and turn on Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841). Open The United States in 1850 bookmark. Click each of the two dashed lines at sea and read its pop-up. Answer: (a) Where did La Amistad start, and where did it end up? (b) Where was the Creole going, and where did the people on board take it instead? (c) What happened to the people on each ship in the end?
6. Routes of escape On the map: In Map layers, turn off the two route layers from questions 4 and 5. Turn on Underground Railroad approximate routes and Underground Railroad cities. Open The Ohio River and the North bookmark. Click the dots on the unshaded land north of the blue states. They lie north of the Great Lakes and along the St. Lawrence River. Read the country in each pop-up. Use Measure to draw a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, in Canada. Chatham is the dot just east of Detroit; click it to check. Answer: (a) Which way do these routes run, compared with the slave trade routes? (b) Name the three cities in Canada. (c) About how far is it in a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, Canada? (d) Ohio was a free state. What does that distance suggest about how safe a free state was for someone who had escaped? Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, Canada: about ________ miles
7. What this map leaves out On the map: Click any Underground Railroad route (a thin green line) and read its pop-up. Think about what you could count or name on this map, and what you could not. Answer: (a) Why does the pop-up call these routes approximate? (b) Name one thing about the people on these routes that the map does not show. (c) What other kind of source would help you find it out?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Which layer changed your picture of 1850 the most when you turned it on, and what did it add?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** free state, slave state, territory, compromise, Missouri Compromise, Compromise of 1850, enslaved, Underground Railroad.
**Standards:** FL SS.8.A.5.2; TX 8.7(D); TX 8.7(E); TX 8.10(A); C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker).
**Languages:** student sheets in English.
**Lesson content version:** 0.10.1, updated 2026-11-11.

### Civil War Battlefields
**Lesson ID:** civil-war-battlefields
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The Civil War. **Time:** About 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open Civil War Battlefields in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=a93738b1850a48308dc797a1cc8352be)
**Description:** Start with the 35 states of 1863 shaded by side, predict where the fighting happened, then turn on the battlefields and the railroads to test the prediction. Students use the pop-ups and Measure to explain why so much of the war was fought in a few places.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Sort the 35 states of 1863 into Union free states, border states and the states that seceded before and after Fort Sumter, using the legend and pop-ups.
- Make and test a prediction about where Civil War battles were fought.
- Measure the distance between Washington and Richmond and use it to explain the cluster of battlefields in Virginia.
- Compare the railroad networks of the two sides and connect railroad junctions and the Mississippi River to where battles were fought.
- Identify what the battlefield layer does not record and name a source that would.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The United States in 1863; Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania; The Mississippi Valley.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Civil War battlefields (off when the map opens): A dark shape for each area the National Park Service maps as a battlefield of the Civil War years. At the national view each one looks like a dot. Almost every pop-up gives the name, the state and the size of the area in acres (two unnamed areas in Oklahoma do not). Off when the map opens; source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program.
- Railroads in operation by 1863 (off when the map opens): Thin black lines for the railroads in operation by 1863. They draw once you zoom in to a region. The pop-up gives the railroad's name (some lines have none), the year it was in operation by and the state. Off when the map opens; source: Jeremy Atack, Historical Geographic Information Systems database of U.S. Railroads.
- The states in the Civil War, 1863: The 35 states of mid-1863 in four groups: Union free state (dark blue), Union slave state or border state (light blue), seceded before Fort Sumter (dark orange) and seceded after Fort Sumter (light orange). The pop-up gives the side, the secession date and, for some states, a note; source: Ordinances of secession and acts of admission; state outlines from Natural Earth.
**What students read before they start:** In 1860 and 1861, eleven states left the United States and formed the Confederate States of America. To secede means to leave a country. The states that stayed were called the Union. The attack on Fort Sumter, in South Carolina, in April 1861 started the fighting. This map shows the country in the middle of 1863.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Blue states stayed in the Union: dark blue for free states, light blue for slave states that stayed (the border states). Orange states seceded: dark orange before Fort Sumter, light orange after. Only the states are on at the start; turn on the other layers in Map layers when a question asks. Dark shapes are battlefields; from far away each one looks like a dot. Thin black lines are railroads, and they appear only after you zoom in to a region. Each state's name is printed on it. Click a state or a battlefield to read its pop-up.
**Compelling question:** By 1863 the United States had split in two. Where was the Civil War fought, and why there?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Two blues, two oranges On the map: Open The United States in 1863 bookmark and open the legend. Count the states in the two orange groups: each state's name is printed on it. The two blue groups are larger: 19 dark blue and 5 light blue. Click South Carolina and Tennessee and read the date each seceded. Answer: (a) How many states seceded before Fort Sumter, and how many after? (b) Which side is blue and which is orange? (c) When did South Carolina secede, and when did Tennessee?
2. Before the dots On the map: Keep only The states in the Civil War, 1863 on. Write your prediction before you turn on any other layer. Answer: Where on this map do you think most Civil War battles were fought: in the blue states, in the orange states, or along the line where they meet? Explain your thinking.
3. Turn on the battlefields On the map: In Map layers, turn on Civil War battlefields. Compare the dots on the blue states with the dots on the orange states. Zoom in on Pennsylvania and click the largest battlefield. Read its pop-up. Look for other battlefields in dark blue states. Answer: (a) Was your prediction right? Which color has most of the battlefields, and which state has the most of all? (b) What is the large battlefield in Pennsylvania, and about how many acres is it? (c) Are there many battlefields in the dark blue states, or few?
4. A hundred miles apart On the map: Open the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark. Find Washington and Richmond. Each was the capital of one side. Use Measure to find the distance between them in miles. Click Maryland, then Virginia, and read the group in each pop-up. Answer: (a) About how far apart are Washington and Richmond? (b) What do you notice about the battlefields between and around them? (c) Maryland and Virginia both touch Washington. Which group is each in, and why would that matter to the United States government? Washington to Richmond: about ________ miles
5. Follow the rails On the map: Stay on the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark. In Map layers, turn on Railroads in operation by 1863. Compare the railroads in Pennsylvania and Ohio with the railroads in Virginia and North Carolina. Zoom in on the battlefields near Manassas and Petersburg and look at the railroads there. Answer: (a) Which side of this view has more railroads? (b) What do you notice about where the Manassas and Petersburg battlefields sit? (c) Why would an army fight for a place where railroads meet?
6. Down the Mississippi On the map: In Map layers, turn off Railroads in operation by 1863. Then open The Mississippi Valley bookmark. Follow the Mississippi River south from Missouri to the Gulf of Mexico. Click three battlefields on the river and write down their names. Find the orange states that lie west of the river. Answer: (a) Name three battlefields on the Mississippi River. (b) Which states that seceded lie west of the river? (c) What would happen to those states if the Union controlled the whole river?
7. What the dots leave out On the map: Open The United States in 1863 bookmark with Civil War battlefields on. Find a battlefield that is not on a shaded state. Zoom in until it is big enough to click, and click it. Read the last sentence of the pop-up. Answer: (a) Where did you find a battlefield outside the shaded states? (b) What does the pop-up tell you about a battle, and what does it leave out? (c) Where could you look to find what is missing?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Which of the three layers changed your mind the most about where the war was fought, and what did it show you?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** secede, Union, Confederacy, border state, Fort Sumter, battlefield, railroad junction.
**Standards:** FL SS.8.A.5.4; TX 8.8(C); TX 8.10(A); TX 8.10(C); C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker).
**Languages:** student sheets in English.
**Lesson content version:** 0.9.1, updated 2026-11-11.

### The Battle of Vicksburg
**Lesson ID:** the-battle-of-vicksburg
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The Civil War. **Time:** About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The Battle of Vicksburg in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=1ba8cd3fc75a49a497be1137fce4c032)
**Description:** Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Social Studies.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Locate Vicksburg on the Mississippi River and follow the railroad east to Jackson to explain why both sides wanted the city.
- Put the key places on Grant's route in order, say which bank of the river each is on, and measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.
- List the battles of the Vicksburg campaign in date order from the Civil War Battlefields pop-ups.
- Identify from the basemap which Confederate states lay west of the Mississippi and what the Union controlled once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had fallen.
- Use evidence from at least two places on the map to explain why the Union needed Vicksburg and how Grant took it.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The Battle of Vicksburg.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg: Places on Grant's route in spring 1863, as dark pins labeled on the map: Miliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards, plus a yellow pin at Vicksburg. No pop-ups; source: Placed by the MapMaker team.
- Railroads 1826 to 1911: Railroads built from 1826 to 1911, so it includes lines built after the war. They draw at the bookmark's view and disappear when zoomed out. Clicking a line opens a list of data fields, including In Operation By (the year); no question uses it; source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team.
- Civil War Battlefields (off when the map opens): Civil War battles as diamonds colored by result. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates and a picture; it does not give the result; source: American Battlefield Trust.
**What students read before they start:** In 1862, Union forces captured New Orleans and Memphis, two cities on the Mississippi River. Between the two, the Confederates still held part of the river, including the city of Vicksburg, Mississippi. In spring 1863, Union General Ulysses S. Grant set out to capture it.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The yellow pin is Vicksburg. Dark pins mark places on Grant's route, each with its name. City and state names, such as Jackson and Louisiana, are part of the basemap. Railroads are thin gray lines with short cross marks, like a track, fainter than the roads; they disappear if you zoom out too far, and they include lines built after the war. Civil War Battlefields is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers. Its diamonds mark battles, colored by who won: use the legend to read the result, because a battle's pop-up gives its name and dates but not the result. If a pop-up shows a broken picture, ignore it.
**Compelling question:** Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Why Vicksburg? On the map: Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Find Vicksburg, the yellow pin on the Mississippi River. Find the railroad line (a thin gray line with cross marks) and follow it east from Vicksburg. If you zoom out and it disappears, zoom back in. Drag the map east to find Jackson, Mississippi, on the basemap (the state capital, east of Vicksburg). Answer: Why would both sides want Vicksburg?
2. Grant's route On the map: Find the dark pins for Milliken's Bend (spelled Miliken's Bend on the map; it is north of Vicksburg, so drag the map down a little if you cannot see it), New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards. Check which side of the river each pin is on. Use Measure for the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend. Answer: Which side of the river is each place on? How far south of Milliken's Bend did Grant cross, and why did he not cross at Vicksburg itself? Measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend: ________ miles
3. The battles of May 1863 On the map: In Map layers, turn on Civil War Battlefields. Click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg and read their dates. Click the diamonds east toward Jackson and read their dates. Answer: Which battles were fought between Bruinsburg Bend, Vicksburg and Jackson? List them in order by date. Did Grant go straight to Vicksburg?
4. Splitting the Confederacy On the map: Zoom out until you can see the Mississippi River from Memphis to the Gulf of Mexico. Keep Civil War Battlefields on and click the diamonds along the river in Louisiana, south of Vicksburg, until a pop-up's title says Port Hudson. It is the last one before the city of Baton Rouge. Read when the siege of Port Hudson ended. Read the state names on the basemap. Answer: When did the siege of Port Hudson end? Which states lie west of the river? What could the Union control once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had both fallen?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Grant crossed the river well south of the city he wanted. What does that tell you about Vicksburg?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** siege, campaign, bluff, gunboat, supply line, surrender.
**Standards:** FL SS.8.A.5.1; TX 8.8(C); TX 8.10(C); C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; C3 D2.His.14.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.9.0, updated 2026-11-11.

### We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791
**Lesson ID:** we-the-people-1787-1791
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Confederation and the Constitution. **Time:** About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=eba1ea7488624f3c88ef094167ed03ca)
**Description:** See how House seats were shared out after the 1790 census, how the three-fifths clause changed the count, and how close each state's vote to ratify was.
**Subjects:** US History, Civics, Government, Data Literacy.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Compare the pie sizes in the Population in 1790 layer to find the most populous state, and read the census line of the pop-ups to identify the states where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved.
- Use the labels and legend of the House seats in 1793 layer to find the states with the most and fewest House seats, and compare each state's House seats with its two senators.
- Read the Virginia and South Carolina pop-ups to compare the seats each actually had with the seats it would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all.
- Read the vote line in the Ratifying the Constitution pop-ups to find the three closest ratification votes and explain why North Carolina has two pies.
- Use population and seat figures from at least two states as evidence for how the three-fifths clause shifted power in the House.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The states in 1790; New England and New York; The South.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Population in 1790: free and enslaved: A pie on each state: free people (blue) and enslaved people (orange-red) in the 1790 census, with bigger pies for more people. Each pop-up, titled with the state's name, gives the total, the number enslaved and the percentage, the number counted under the three-fifths clause, the state's House seats in 1793, its two senators, and the seats it would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all; source: U.S. Census Bureau, 1790 census and apportionment ratio; Apportionment Act of April 14, 1792 (National Archives); state outlines from Natural Earth.
- House seats in 1793 (off when the map opens): States shaded from pale to dark blue by their House seats under the apportionment act of 14 April 1792 (legend: 1 to 2, 4 to 6, 7 to 10, 13 to 19 seats), labeled with the state's abbreviation and seats. Same pop-up as the population layer; source: National Archives.
- House seats today (2020 apportionment) (off when the map opens): Each state's House seats after the 2020 census; source: U.S. Census Bureau (MapMaker catalogue).
- Ratifying the Constitution, 1787–1791 (off when the map opens): A pie where each state's ratifying convention met: votes to ratify (blue) and against (orange-red), with bigger pies for more delegates. Labels give the state and the order it ratified (DE 1 to VT 14). Each pop-up gives the result, date and vote, where the convention met, and a note. North Carolina has two pies: its first convention, at Hillsborough in 1788 (label NC (1788)), did not ratify; source: Center for the Study of the American Constitution, University of Wisconsin–Madison (votes, dates and meeting places).
**What students read before they start:** In 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution. Large and small states disagreed about how many votes each should have in Congress. They settled it with the Great Compromise, and with the Three-Fifths Compromise on how enslaved people were counted. The Constitution would take effect only when nine states had ratified it, each at a special convention.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The map has no place names: click a pie or a state to see its name in the pop-up title. Pies on the states show the people in 1790: blue for free, orange-red for enslaved (the legend names each color), and bigger pies for more people. Three layers are off when the map opens. In House seats in 1793, darker blue means more seats, and each label gives the state's abbreviation and seats. In Ratifying the Constitution, each pie sits where a state's convention met: blue for votes to ratify, orange-red for votes against, and labels give the order each state ratified. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia.
**Compelling question:** Who was counted in the new Constitution, and how close did it come to being rejected?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Who lived where in 1790? On the map: Open The states in 1790 bookmark. Click the pies and read each pop-up. Read the first line of each pop-up, which gives the percentage enslaved. If the percentage has many decimal places, round it to a whole number. Answer: Which state had the most people? In which states were more than a quarter of the people enslaved?
2. Seats in Congress On the map: In Map layers, turn on House seats in 1793. Read the labels: each gives the state and its seats, and darker blue means more seats. A small state may have no label: click it to read its seats. Click two states and read how many senators each had. Answer: Which state had the most seats in the House of Representatives, and which the fewest? How many senators did each of your two states have? Why do you think the House and the Senate are counted differently?
3. The three-fifths clause On the map: Click Virginia and South Carolina. Read the seats in 1793 in each pop-up, then the paragraph that begins "If enslaved people had been counted in full": it gives the seats with a full count, and with no count at all. Click other states and compare the same three numbers. Answer: Under the three-fifths clause, three of every five enslaved people were counted when House seats were shared out. How many seats did Virginia and South Carolina each have under the clause, and how many would each have had if enslaved people had been counted in full, or not at all? Which states gained seats by counting enslaved people, who could not vote? Virginia: ____ seats with the three-fifths clause; ____ if counted in full; ____ if not counted at all. South Carolina: ____; ____; ____.
4. How close was ratification? On the map: In Map layers, turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793. Turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Click the pies and read the first line of each pop-up: the votes for and against. Find North Carolina and click both of its pies. Answer: Which three votes were closest? Why does North Carolina have two pies?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Which number on this map surprised you most, and why?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** ratify, convention, census, apportionment, Great Compromise, three-fifths clause, Federalist, Anti-Federalist.
**Standards:** TX 8.4(D); TX 8.17(A); FL SS.8.A.3.10; FL SS.8.A.3.11; C3 D2.Civ.5.6-8; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.9.0, updated 2026-11-11.

### Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live
**Lesson ID:** rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Confederation and the Constitution. **Time:** About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=59467ac7d7c64542acaa6a3e9c19ebf4)
**Description:** Map the public places in your own community where people use the rights in the Bill of Rights and carry out their responsibilities as citizens, and find who represents your district in Congress.
**Subjects:** US History, Civics, Government, Geography.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Zoom to their own town, click inside their congressional district to read the representative's name, party and district number, and count the districts in their state.
- Use the Topographic basemap labels to find four public places in their community and sketch a labeled pin on each with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there.
- Add pins for places where people carry out responsibilities as citizens, and sort those responsibilities into required by law and voluntary.
- Turn on the National Register of Historic Places layer, identify the two listed places nearest the school using the pop-up address and the basemap, and connect one public building to a right or responsibility.
- Use the places they pinned as evidence to explain where in their community rights and responsibilities are exercised.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The United States.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Congressional districts (119th Congress): District boundaries for the 119th Congress (2025–2027) as blue outlines, current as of the layer's last update (see its item page); representatives change at elections and in special elections. Each pop-up reads "[Representative Name] ([Party]) represents [State] Congressional District [number]"; source: Esri; U.S. Census Bureau; Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives (MapMaker catalogue).
- National Register of Historic Places (off when the map opens): Places on the National Register as diamonds colored by type: building, structure, district, site or object. They appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up starts with the place's name in bold, then its address, city, county and state, the resource type and a link to the National Archives record; source: National Park Service (MapMaker catalogue).
**What students read before they start:** In 1791, ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, were added to the Constitution. They protect rights such as freedom of speech, religion and the press, the right to gather peacefully, and the right to a fair trial. Citizens also have responsibilities to their community and their country.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The Topographic basemap has place and street names. When you zoom in close it names some public buildings, but not all of them, so you may need to use what you know about your town. Blue lines are the boundaries of congressional districts for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); click inside one to see who represents it. National Register of Historic Places is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers and zoom in to see its diamonds, colored by type of place (see the legend). Its pop-ups give each place's name and address. Put your pins on public places, not homes. Sketches are not saved when you close the map.
**Compelling question:** Where in our community do people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Who represents us? On the map: Zoom to your town; the basemap has place names. Find the blue lines, which are the boundaries of congressional districts. Your state's border is drawn the same way. Click inside your district and read the pop-up. Zoom out to see your whole state. To count its districts, click inside each area in your state and read the district number in the pop-up. Answer: Who represents your district in the House of Representatives, which party do they belong to, and what is the district's number? How many districts does your state have?
2. Rights in public places On the map: Zoom in on your town until you can read the street names. Find four public places, not homes: a courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place or newspaper office. If the map does not name a place, use what you know about where it is. Use Sketch to put a pin on each one. Next to each pin, write a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there. Finish in one lesson or take a screenshot, because sketches are not saved. Answer: Which four places did you pin, and which right from the Bill of Rights do people use at each?
3. Responsibilities On the map: Start at the courthouse or city hall you pinned. Add a pin at each place where people carry out a civic responsibility: voting, jury service, paying taxes. Next to each pin, write the responsibility. Answer: Which places did you pin, and which responsibility do people carry out at each?
4. History where we live On the map: In Map layers, turn on National Register of Historic Places. Zoom in until the diamonds appear and click the two nearest your school; the pop-up gives each place's name and address. Read Resource Type in the pop-up, or use the legend, to tell a building from a district or a site. Answer: Is either a public building, such as a courthouse, post office, school or library? Which right or responsibility does it connect with?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** What did the map show you about your own community that you hadn't noticed before?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** amendment, Bill of Rights, civil liberties, citizen, responsibility, congressional district, representative, jury.
**Standards:** TX 8.19(B); TX 8.19(C); FL SS.8.CG.2.5; C3 D2.Civ.2.6-8; C3 D2.Civ.8.6-8; C3 D2.Geo.1.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.8.0, updated 2026-11-11.

### The First Political Parties, 1796–1800
**Lesson ID:** presidential-elections-1796-1800
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The early republic. **Time:** About 57 minutes: 47 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The First Political Parties, 1796–1800 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=6173219d9cd84812bcd4fed859b2c182)
**Description:** Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and work out whether one state decided the election of 1800.
**Subjects:** US History, Government, Civics, Geography.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 layer to describe which regions voted mostly for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the split states for their numbers.
- Switch between the 1796 and 1800 layers to find the state whose whole pie changed color and the states whose shares changed.
- Read the two-color pies in the Election of 1800 layer to identify the closest state.
- Use New York's electors and the split states in the Election of 1800 layer to work out whether one state decided the election.
- Use the pattern of electors' votes across the sixteen states as evidence to describe where each party was strong in 1800.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The sixteen states.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Election of 1796: electors' votes: A pie on each of the 16 states: electors' votes for John Adams (Federalist, orange) and Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican, blue), with bigger pies for more electors. Each pop-up lists the votes for each main candidate, with the rest grouped as others; source: National Archives (Electoral College results); state outlines from Natural Earth.
- Election of 1800: electors' votes (off when the map opens): The same for 1800. Each pop-up lists every candidate's votes and explains the Jefferson–Burr tie and the 12th Amendment, so no question asks for those; source: National Archives (Electoral College results); state outlines from Natural Earth.
- Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819: Pink squares for Marbury v. Madison (1803, Washington, D.C.) and McCulloch v. Maryland (1819, Baltimore), labeled with the case name and year. Each pop-up gives the question, the ruling, why it matters and why it's placed there (Why here); source: National Archives (Milestone Documents).
**What students read before they start:** George Washington belonged to no party, and in 1796, as he prepared to leave office, he warned Americans against parties. By then two had formed: the Federalists, led by John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republicans, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Each elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The map has no place names: click a pie to see the state's name and its number of electors. An elector is a person chosen by a state to vote for president. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted: orange for John Adams (Federalist) and blue for Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican); use the legend. Bigger pies mean more electors. Each elector cast two votes; the pop-up lists the other candidates. Election of 1800 is off when the map opens. Pink squares mark two Supreme Court cases; this lesson does not use them, and they cover Maryland's pie, so turn that layer off in Map layers. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia, and territories aren't shown.
**Compelling question:** How did the first political parties divide the country?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. The election of 1796 On the map: Open The sixteen states bookmark. In Map layers, turn off Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819: its pink squares cover Maryland's pie. Use the legend to read the 1796 pies. Click each two-color pie and read its pop-up. Maryland's says 10 electors but lists 7 for Adams and 4 for Jefferson: each elector cast two votes, so a state's votes add up to twice its electors. Answer: Which part of the country mostly voted for Adams, and which for Jefferson? Which states split their votes, and how?
2. The election of 1800 On the map: In Map layers, turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800. Find the two-color pies. Click each one and read how its electors divided. Answer: Which states have two-color pies this time? How did each one's electors divide between Adams and Jefferson? Which state was the closest?
3. Which states switched? On the map: In Map layers, switch between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 (one on, one off). Find the state whose whole pie changed from orange to blue, and click it to read its electors. Find the states whose pies changed their shares, and check New England. Answer: Which state's whole pie changed from orange to blue, and how many electors did it have? Which states' pies changed their shares, and did any New England state change? Using both maps, where was each party strong and where did the two parties compete? Changed completely: ____________, with ____ electors.
4. Did one state decide the election? On the map: In Map layers, make sure Election of 1800 is on. Click New York and read how many electors it had and how they voted in 1800. Then turn on Election of 1796, turn off Election of 1800, and read how New York voted in 1796. Click the two-color pies again and read how close each state was. Answer: In 1800 Jefferson won 73 electors' votes and Adams 65. If New York had voted as it did in 1796, what would the totals have been? Which other states were close enough to change the result? With New York: Adams ____, Jefferson ____.
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** If you could have changed the result in one state in 1800, which would you pick, and why that one?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** political party, Federalist, Democratic-Republican, elector, Electoral College, 12th Amendment, judicial review, implied powers.
**Standards:** TX 8.5(D); FL SS.8.A.3.13; FL SS.8.A.3.14.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.9.0, updated 2026-11-11.

### The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806
**Lesson ID:** louisiana-purchase-1803-1806
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The early republic. **Time:** About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=f8af7269e5c14e69b060d6184d04ff85)
**Description:** Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Indigenous Studies, Economics.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the legend to compare the Louisiana Purchase with the land of 1783 and read the purchase pop-up for its size and price.
- Use the United States Watersheds layer to name the Ohio and Missouri watersheds and trace on the basemap where their rivers reach the sea.
- Follow the Lewis and Clark trail and campsites up the Missouri and use the Biomes layer to name the biomes the expedition crossed.
- Find where the trail leaves the Louisiana Purchase and measure the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific coast.
- Use the watershed boundaries and river routes as evidence to explain why New Orleans mattered to farmers west of the Appalachians.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The Louisiana Purchase; Up the Missouri; Across the Rockies to the Pacific.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Territorial acquisitions to 1803: The land Britain gave up in 1783 (green) and the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 (yellow). Edges of the purchase that were settled later are in other colors or stripes: with Britain in 1818, and with Texas in 1845 and the Mexican Cession in 1848. Each pop-up gives a short note; source: MapMaker catalogue (US territorial acquisitions).
- Biomes (off when the map opens): Today's biomes, shaded by type; each pop-up names the biome (first line), the realm and the ecoregion (a modern reference layer, not a historical reconstruction); source: RESOLVE Ecoregions 2017, via Esri (MapMaker catalogue).
- United States Watersheds (off when the map opens): River basins outlined in brown, from the 22 largest regions (Hydrologic Unit Code 2s, such as Ohio Region and Missouri Region) down to small watersheds as you zoom in; each pop-up names the basin and lists the states it touches (a modern reference layer, not a historical reconstruction); source: U.S. Geological Survey Watershed Boundary Dataset, via Esri (MapMaker catalogue).
- Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail: The National Park Service's line of the expedition's route, about 4,900 miles from Pittsburgh to the mouth of the Columbia River. No pop-up: the line has no information to click; source: National Park Service, Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail.
- Lewis and Clark campsites (approximate): Approximate places where the Corps of Discovery camped, 1803–1806. No pop-up: the symbols have no information to click; source: National Park Service, from Robert Bergantino, Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology.
**What students read before they start:** In 1803 the United States bought France's claim to a huge area west of the Mississippi River. Native nations lived on and governed most of that land; the National Park Service says the expedition met more than 50 Tribal Nations. President Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, to explore it and look for a water route to the Pacific Ocean. The expedition set out in 1803 and returned in 1806.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The map has no place names: click an area to see its name. Use the legend: the darker gray-green land east of the Mississippi is the land Britain gave up to the United States in 1783; yellow is the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Edges of the purchase settled later have other colors or stripes. A purple line follows the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, and symbols mark the Corps' approximate campsites, close enough together to cover parts of the line; the line and the symbols have no pop-ups. United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens and show today's landscape. Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in.
**Compelling question:** What did the Louisiana Purchase add to the United States, and why did the Mississippi River matter so much?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. A bigger country On the map: Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark and use the legend. Compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the darker land east of it, the United States in 1783. Click the Louisiana Purchase and read its pop-up. Answer: About how much bigger did the country become? How much land was the Louisiana Purchase, and what did it cost? Size: about ____ million acres. Price: $____ million.
2. Why New Orleans? On the map: In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the large brown outline that the orange campsite dots cross in the yellow land, and read the first line of its pop-up. Then do the same for the outline the dots cross farther east, in the dark land. Each region is named for its river. Both rivers flow into the Mississippi. Zoom out and find where the land reaches into the Gulf of Mexico at the bottom of the yellow area: that is the river's mouth. Answer: Which river regions are the two outlines? Into which big river do they flow, and which city sits near its mouth? In 1800 farmers west of the Appalachians sent their crops to market by river: why did control of New Orleans matter to them?
3. Up the Missouri On the map: Open the Up the Missouri bookmark. Follow the trail line and the campsite symbols up the Missouri River. In Map layers, turn off United States Watersheds and turn on Biomes. Click the shading along the route and read the first line of the pop-up. Look at where the campsites sit. Answer: Which biome covers the Great Plains? Why do you think the Corps traveled along rivers?
4. Across the Rockies On the map: In Map layers, turn off Biomes, then open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark. Find where the line of campsite dots leaves the yellow Louisiana Purchase. Zoom out and find Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where the Ohio River begins: it is where the continuous line of dots ends in the east. Ignore the few scattered dots beyond it. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the trail's western end on the Pacific coast. Answer: In what kind of land does the trail leave the Louisiana Purchase (plains, mountains or coast)? Was the Pacific coast part of the purchase? What is the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific end of the trail? Straight-line distance: ________ miles. The trail itself is about 4,900 miles long.
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** The United States bought this land from France. Before you start says the Corps of Discovery met more than 50 Tribal Nations along the way. Whose land was it, and what does the map leave out?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** Louisiana Purchase, Corps of Discovery, expedition, watershed, river basin, biome, Continental Divide, Tribal Nation.
**Standards:** TX 8.6(B); TX 8.10(A); TX 8.10(C); FL SS.8.A.3.14; FL SS.8.G.1.2; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Measure with MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/measure-with-mapmaker); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.10.0, updated 2026-11-11.

### The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823
**Lesson ID:** war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** The early republic. **Time:** About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=fad1cdb9d5704401a4e05c34f7ee693c)
**Description:** Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography, Government.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Use the battle diamonds in the Battles of the War of 1812 layer to identify the three main areas of fighting.
- Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.
- Read the pop-ups of the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line layers to describe what the treaty settled.
- Compare the dates of independence and US recognition in the Latin American independence layer with Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.
- Use the locations of the battles and the 1819 boundary as evidence to explain how the United States' position in North America changed between 1812 and 1823.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The War of 1812; The 1819 boundary; Latin America in 1825.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Historic National Boundaries: 1800: Borders in 1800, before the Louisiana Purchase, with the United States shaded pink. Each pop-up names the country; source: University of Minnesota (historic national boundaries), from the MapMaker catalogue.
- Land Spain gave up in 1819 (off when the map opens): Land Spain gave up in the Adams–Onís Treaty, including East and West Florida (green). Each pop-up gives a short note; source: MapMaker catalogue (US territorial acquisitions).
- Battlefield Boundaries: War of 1812: The land each battlefield covered (tan) and its core area (lighter tan). It draws only when zoomed in close to a battle. Each pop-up gives the battle and its size in acres; source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program.
- Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 (off when the map opens): The 1819 boundary with Spain as a pink dashed line in seven parts, drawn from the treaty's description and approximate. Each pop-up describes its part; source: Treaty text from the Avalon Project, Yale Law School; drawn on Natural Earth rivers.
- Battles of the War of 1812: 52 battles from 1811 to 1815 as diamonds: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if inconclusive; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. Each pop-up gives the dates, the victor, total casualties, a short account and a casualties chart; it does not show the state or the leaders. The legend labels every opponent of the United States as British, but some battles were fought against Native nations: Tippecanoe (the Shawnee-led confederacy), Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend (Red Stick Creeks). The pop-up's account says who fought; source: American Battlefield Trust (War of 1812 Battles map).
- Latin American independence and US recognition (off when the map opens): Ten Latin American nations, labeled with the year of independence: blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824, orange diamonds if it recognized them later (1826 to 1862). Each pop-up gives the capital, today's countries, independence and recognition; source: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State; Library of Congress country studies.
**What students read before they start:** In the early 1800s Britain and France were at war, and both seized American ships. British warships also forced sailors off American ships into the Royal Navy, and Britain supported Native nations resisting American settlement. In June 1812 the United States declared war on Britain.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** The names printed on the map are from 1800, such as New Spain and Indiana Territory, and there are no city names: click a feature to see its name. Pink shading shows the United States in 1800. Diamonds mark battles; use the legend: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if neither side won; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. The legend says British for every opponent, but some battles were fought against Native nations: the pop-up's story tells you who fought. Each battle pop-up gives the dates, the victor and the casualties. Tan shading shows battlefield land when you zoom in close to a battle. Three layers are off when the map opens: the land Spain gave up in 1819 (green), the treaty line (pink dashes, in seven parts) and the Latin American nations, shown as blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824 and orange diamonds if later; the pop-up gives the exact date.
**Compelling question:** How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Where was the war fought? On the map: Open The War of 1812 bookmark. Click some diamonds in each group and read their pop-ups. Answer: In which three areas was most of the fighting?
2. The biggest battles On the map: Click the three biggest diamonds. Zoom in on the Niagara River, between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, where several large diamonds sit close together. Read when each battle was fought and who won. Work out where from the map and the pop-up's account. Compare each battle's date with December 24, 1814, when the peace treaty was signed at Ghent. Answer: Where and when was each battle fought, and who won? Which big battle came after the peace treaty?
3. Florida and a new border On the map: Open The 1819 boundary bookmark. In Map layers, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819. Click the green land and read its pop-up. Drag the map east to see all of Florida. Click each part of the pink dashed line and read its pop-up. Answer: What did the United States gain from Spain? Where does the new border follow rivers, and where does it follow straight lines? Why might a border switch from one to the other?
4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine On the map: Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark. Turn on Latin American independence and US recognition. Click the blue circles and read each recognition date in the pop-up. The year printed beside a name on the map is the year of independence, not recognition. The pop-up may show the date with a clock time, one day early; that does not change your answer. Check each date against December 2, 1823 (blue only means recognized by 1824). Answer: Which nations had the United States recognized before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823? Why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out of the Americas?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** The war itself changed no borders. Which layer on this map shows the biggest change, and what caused it?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** impressment, blockade, Treaty of Ghent, cession, boundary, recognition, Monroe Doctrine, independence.
**Standards:** TX 8.5(E); TX 8.5(F); FL SS.8.A.4.1; C3 D2.His.1.6-8; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data); [Sketch on a Map](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/sketch-on-a-map).
**Languages:** student sheets in English and Spanish.
**Lesson content version:** 0.8.0, updated 2026-11-11.

### Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894
**Lesson ID:** land-cessions-1784-1894
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Age of Jackson. **Time:** About 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question.
