**MapMaker map:** [Open Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894 in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=fd8f742aec1c4a8a9648cd20dafffe11)
**Description:** Turn on one period at a time to watch American Indian land cessions spread across the United States, predict where the next ones will be, and explain why the 1830s cessions are where they are. The map is Charles Royce's record of cessions, so students also ask whose view it shows.
**Subjects:** US History, Geography.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Describe where the United States had gained American Indian land before 1830, using the Cessions dated before 1830 layer and the legend.
- Make a prediction about the next period from the map, then turn on the 1830s layer and test it.
- Read the nation, date and kind of document in the pop-ups of three 1830s cessions in the Southeast.
- Explain the 1830s pattern in the Southeast using the Indian Removal Act (1830) as evidence.
- Evaluate the map as a source: who recorded the cessions, when, and whose view is missing.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The United States; The Southeast; The Old Northwest; The Plains and the West.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 (off when the map opens): Green areas: cessions with a date from 1840 to 1894. Off when the map opens; source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899).
- Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (off when the map opens): Orange areas: cessions with a date in the 1830s, the decade of the Indian Removal Act. Off when the map opens; source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899).
- Cessions dated before 1830: Light blue areas: cessions with a date from 1784 to 1829; source: USDA Forest Service, from Charles C. Royce's maps and schedule (Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899).
**What students read before they start:** A treaty is a written agreement between nations. A cession is land a nation gives up, usually in a treaty. On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. It let the President make treaties to move American Indian nations from east of the Mississippi River to land in the West. In December 1830, Jackson told Congress that removal meant "opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites." The map comes from records Charles Royce made from government documents. The government published them in 1899.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Light blue: cessions dated before 1830. Orange: 1830 to 1839. Green: 1840 to 1894. Only light blue is on at the start; turn on the others in Map layers when a question asks. Where layers overlap, the colors mix: click the area to read its dates. Some areas have two or more dates. The first date can be a treaty that kept the land for the nation, so read every date. Click an area to open its pop-up; scroll to see all of it.
**Compelling question:** How did the United States gain American Indian land between 1784 and 1894, and why did the pattern change in the 1830s?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Notice: before 1830 On the map: Open The United States bookmark. Find the light blue areas (Cessions dated before 1830) in the legend and on the map. Zoom in one or two steps until the state names show. Open The Southeast bookmark and look for gaps: places in Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia with no light blue. Answer: (a) Name three states where the United States gained land before 1830. (b) Name one big part of the United States with no light blue. (c) Which Southeast states have gaps with no light blue?
2. Predict On the map: Keep only Cessions dated before 1830 on. Look at the gaps you found in the Southeast, and at the empty parts east and west of the Mississippi River (the long river that runs down the middle of the country to the Gulf of Mexico). Write your prediction before you turn on any other layer. Answer: Where do you expect the cessions of the 1830s to be? Why there? I predict the 1830s cessions will be in ______________ because ______________.
3. Reveal: the 1830s On the map: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (orange). Open The Southeast bookmark, then The Old Northwest bookmark (the Great Lakes states). Compare the orange areas (Cessions dated 1830 to 1839) with your prediction. Answer: (a) Name three states with orange areas (Cessions dated 1830 to 1839). (b) Was your prediction right? (c) What happened to the gaps you found in the Southeast in question 1?
4. Explain why On the map: Make sure Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (orange) is on, and open The Southeast bookmark. Click three orange areas: the large one in the middle of Mississippi, north-east of Jackson; in Alabama north of Montgomery, near the Georgia line; in the north-west corner of Georgia. For each one, write the nation (the title of the pop-up), the date in the 1830s, and the words on the first link (for example Treaty text). You don't need to open the link. Answer: (a) Fill in the nation, date and link words for each area. (b) In December 1830 Jackson told Congress that removal meant "opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites." Using his words and the Indian Removal Act (Before you start), why might these cessions have come in the 1830s, and why here? Mississippi: ________ , ________ , ________ Alabama: ________ , ________ , ________ Georgia: ________ , ________ , ________
5. Reveal: 1840 to 1894 On the map: In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 (green). Open The United States bookmark, then The Plains and the West bookmark. Answer: (a) Where are most of the green areas (Cessions dated 1840 to 1894)? (b) Name one part of the United States with no cessions at all on this map.
6. Question the source On the map: Click the orange area in the north-west corner of Georgia (Cherokee). Scroll to the end of the pop-up and read the note in slanted letters. Click the orange area in Alabama north of Montgomery (Creek) and read Nations today. Answer: (a) Who recorded these cessions, and from whose records? (b) What is missing from the Creek pop-up? (c) In 1836, 3,352 Cherokees signed a petition saying the treaty was made "without any authority from the council or people of the Nation." How does that change how you read the Cherokee pop-up?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Turning the layers on one at a time, what did you notice about how the cessions spread that you might have missed on a finished map?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
**Key words:** treaty, cession, Indian Removal Act, removal, petition, primary source.
**Standards:** C3 D2.His.14.6-8; C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8; TX 8.5(H); TX 8.10(A); FL SS.8.A.4.4.
**How-to pages for the tools this lesson uses:** [Navigating MapMaker](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/navigating-mapmaker); [Explore Layers and Data](https://mapmaker-support-hub-mpmkr.hub.arcgis.com/pages/explore-layers-and-data).
**Languages:** student sheets in English.
**Lesson content version:** 0.5.0, updated 2026-11-09.

### The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote
**Lesson ID:** election-1828-right-to-vote
**Subject:** History. **Course:** US History. **Grade:** 8. **Unit:** Age of Jackson. **Time:** About 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question.
**MapMaker map:** [Open The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote in MapMaker](https://mpmkr.maps.arcgis.com/apps/instant/atlas/index.html?appid=0cd1cdee853c413a84bfe4b9a6931f0d&webmap=1bd912453059450dac83074ea42e5424)
**Description:** See how each state's electors voted in 1828, then turn on who could vote there: the property and tax rules for white men, and whether free Black men could vote. Students test the idea that Jackson's election was a victory for the common man against the rules state by state.
**Subjects:** US History, Civics, Geography.
**Learning objectives (students will):**
- Describe the result of the 1828 election by region using the pies, legend and pop-ups.
- Make and test a prediction about where white men had to own property or pay a tax to vote.
- Compare the rules for white men and for free Black men in the same states, including New York.
- Explain what expanded suffrage meant in 1828 and for whom, using evidence from the pop-ups.
- Distinguish what the law said from what happened, using Pennsylvania as an example.
**Bookmarks in this map:** The 24 states of 1828; New England and New York; The Middle Atlantic.
**Layers in this map (exact name: what students see; source):**
- Election of 1828: electors' votes: A pie on each of the 24 states: electors' votes for Andrew Jackson (blue) and John Quincy Adams (orange), with bigger pies for more electors. The pop-up gives the votes, who chose the electors and both voting rules, with sources; source: National Archives (Electoral College results, 1828); state outlines from Natural Earth.
- Free Black men and the vote, 1828 (off when the map opens): Each state shaded pink by whether free Black men could vote: light pink, could vote on the same terms as white men; middle pink, only with extra rules or kept out in practice; dark pink, could not vote. Off when the map opens; source: State constitutions and laws, as cited in each pop-up.
- White men and the vote, 1828 (off when the map opens): Each state shaded green by its rule for white men: light green, no property or tax rule; middle green, had to pay a tax or meet a similar rule (militia service, road work or a little land); dark green, had to own property. Off when the map opens; source: State constitutions and laws, as cited in each pop-up.
**What students read before they start:** In 1828, Americans did not vote for the president directly. Each state chose electors, and the electors voted for president. Andrew Jackson ran against President John Quincy Adams. Each state made its own rules about who could vote. Some states made men own land or pay a tax to vote. Suffrage means the right to vote. A legislature is a state's lawmakers. The militia was a state's citizen soldiers.
**How the student sheet explains the map's symbols:** Blue pies: electors for Andrew Jackson. Orange pies: John Quincy Adams. Bigger pies mean more electors. Only the pies are on at the start; turn on the other layers in Map layers when a question asks. The white men layer is green and the free Black men layer is pink. In both, lighter means fewer limits and darker means more; the legend gives each shade its meaning in words. The key for these layers is lower down in the legend: scroll to see it. Click a state to read its votes, its rules and the sources; scroll to see all of the pop-up.
**Compelling question:** Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 is often called a victory for the common man. Who could vote in 1828, and did it depend on where you lived?
**Questions already in this lesson:**
1. Notice: the result On the map: Open The 24 states of 1828 bookmark and open the legend. Find the blue pies (Andrew Jackson) and the orange pies (John Quincy Adams). Click the two-color pies and read the votes in each pop-up. Answer: (a) Which parts of the country voted mostly for Adams, and which for Jackson? (b) Which three states split their electors?
2. Predict On the map: Keep only Election of 1828: electors' votes on. Write your predictions before you turn on any other layer. Answer: (a) Where do you think white men still had to own property or pay a tax to vote? (b) Where do you think free Black men could vote? Give a reason for each. I predict ______________ because ______________.
3. Reveal: white men On the map: In Map layers, turn on White men and the vote, 1828. Scroll down the legend to its key: light green means no property or tax rule, middle green means pay a tax (or a similar rule), dark green means own property. Click a dark state and a light state and read White men in each pop-up. Rhode Island is small: use the New England and New York bookmark. Answer: (a) Which two states are shaded dark? (b) Where are the light states (no rule)? (c) Did Jackson win only in states with no rule? Was your prediction right?
4. Reveal: free Black men On the map: In Map layers, turn off White men and the vote, 1828 and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828. Scroll down the legend to its key and find the lightest states, labeled Could vote. Open the New England and New York bookmark, click New York and read White men and Free Black men. Answer: (a) Name the states where free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men. (b) How were New York's rules for white men and for Black men different? (c) Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri had no property or tax rule for white men. What does this layer show for free Black men there?
5. Explain why On the map: Click South Carolina and read Who chose the electors. Click Georgia, the state south of it, and read the same line. Open The Middle Atlantic bookmark, click Delaware and read Who chose the electors. Answer: (a) Who chose the electors in South Carolina and Delaware? (b) What changed in Georgia in 1828? (c) In South Carolina and Delaware, could a man who met the voting rules vote for president? What does that add to your answer about who could vote?
6. Question the source On the map: Click Pennsylvania and read Free Black men. Read the sentence about women in slanted letters near the end of any pop-up, just above the last link. Answer: (a) In Pennsylvania, how was what happened different from what the law said? (b) Which people does the map not show? (c) What else would you need to find out how many people actually voted in 1828?
**Closing reflection already in this lesson:** Turning on the rules one layer at a time, what did you notice about who could vote that a list of election results would not show?
**Answers:** not in this file. The answers are on the lesson's teacher page, for teachers only; do not give answers to the questions above, and do not write student material that contains them.
